2. **Fairness.** Among patients of the **same level**, the one who has waited longest (counted from arrival day) should go first, whichever department they are in. Among clinically acceptable alternatives, prefer the more equitable one, even at a moderate efficiency cost.
3. **Efficiency.** Use beds and nurses without unnecessary idle capacity or imbalance, subject to the two objectives above.

No department has priority over another. A patient's priority depends on their level, not their department.

content.text:
Today's decision (day 23) was accepted on the first attempt.

**Situation:** The bed pool fell by 40 to 56, an external event. Occupied beds total 62, so the shock exception applies and exactly 6 occupied beds had to be removed.

**Allocation submitted:**

| Department | Beds | Nurses |
|---|---|---|
| Cardiology | 16 | 9 |
| Internal medicine | 20 | 14 |
| Neurology | 12 | 8 |
| Orthopedics | 8 | 6 |

**Why this allocation:**
- **Beds:** The 6 removed beds are the six held by level-1 patients, the lowest level: 1 in cardiology, 4 in internal medicine and 1 in orthopedics. No higher-level patient loses a bed while a lower-level patient keeps one. I worked out who holds beds from census minus the overflow queue, and the simulation matched.
- **Nurses:** Each department gets its requirement, so no level is short. The one spare nurse goes to internal medicine, which has the largest census and overflow.
- **Alternative rejected:** I also simulated moving one bed from neurology to cardiology (17/20/11/8). It would have cut a neurology level-2 patient's bed while a cardiology level-1 patient kept one. That patient had been waiting 4 days.

**Cost:** Some new level-2 and level-3 arrivals stay in overflow today. Every bed is held by a level-2 or level-3 patient, and the rules forbid removing more than the 6-bed shortfall. That is 2 level-3 and 3 level-2 patients in internal medicine, 1 level-3 and 1 level-2 in neurology, and 2 level-2 in orthopedics.

I didn't change any files.
